results.title: Cheers erupt as woman pulled from rubble in Colombia after 36 hours
D. None of the Above: An unwelcome invitation to diseases of the past
results.description: By Daniel Dunaief They are perplexed, frustrated, angry and concerned. Local doctors have seen no reason to follow the Executive Order issued by President Donald Trump which suggests a reduction in childhood vaccines to 11 from 17. Cutting back on vaccines like Hepatitis B can have serious consequences, they say, as children who contract this liver virus can go on to develop lifelong health challenges. The new recommendations don’t come with a new set of data, facts, or analysis. They are as confusing as they are problematic, as doctors from the American Academy of Pediatrics to members of the Republican Party have urged Americans to protect themselves and their children with vaccinations that save lives. Do shots hurt in the moment? Sure. But then, why would the newest recommendation urge people to separate the well-established combination of measles, mumps and rubella into three different shots? Amid the many concerns doctors shared, one remains practical: such so-called monovalent shots aren’t available. A patient walking into a pediatrician’s office to get a shot only for measles will receive blank looks from the doctor, the nurse and the lady with the alligator purse. No, they’ll say, that’s not an option. And, even if it were, how many people want to bring their child to the doctor’s office more frequently to get additional separate shots? The flu shots work. No, they don’t prevent people from getting sick. And yes, people probably know someone who has received the shot and still struggled with symptoms for days on end. They also probably know people who never got shots and are strong as a horse. But in most cases, these shots reduce the severity and duration of symptoms. Some doctors suggested checking with the parents of their children’s friends on their vaccination status. If another child isn’t receiving necessary vaccinations, they urged people to limit the exposure to that child. While that seems socially awkward and could start separating children into groups in ways akin to the echo chamber worlds of their parents, it underscores how seriously these health care providers take the threat from illnesses and the lengths they are prepared to go to protect their children and families. The decisions people make about vaccinations affect a much larger group than just their children. Those same delightful and energetic youngest members of their families live in the equivalent of a school petri dish, where they touch the same toys, share the same books, walk through the same hallways and grab the same doorknobs going into and out of classrooms. They then come home and give their grandparents hugs, shake their hands for receiving awards or distinctions, and throw balls back and forth. Each of these interactions gives them a chance to share more than a good time, as the microbes in their system readily jump from them to anyone else in the room. How have we reached the point where health care decisions have become political? Why would one group of people become more beholden to the data or science than another? There’s no new information that suggests that people should change their vaccination habits. There is speculation, as people have suggested, without proof, that higher diagnosed rates of autism somehow connects to a more rigorous vaccine schedule. By that logic, maybe climate change isn’t causing heat waves, thunderstorms and violent weather, but, rather high vaccination rates are the culprit. Maybe fewer shots will help refreeze glaciers. More people are diagnosed with autism in large part because of the greater attention to it. It’s become more widely recognized and accepted to diagnose people. As members of any community, we make decisions that affect us and our neighbors. When we don’t protect ourselves and our children, we give illnesses an opportunity to jump from one of us to the next, making herd immunity less likely. Dr. Sharon Nachman, chief of the division of pediatric infectious diseases at Stony Brook Children’s Hospital, suggested that people wouldn’t ask a car mechanic to fix a bathroom. They would, and should, however, ask doctors to help them make informed decisions about the health of their children and the community. The American Academy of Pediatrics, New York State and numerous other states have urged people to benefit from vaccines that work. Important decisions should follow rigorous testing. At this point, cutting back on vaccines based on hunches and correlations creates conditions that endanger families and communities. People should ask doctors they trust to help them choose a course of action for their beloved children. Your doctors, neighbors, friends, family and fellow community members will appreciate the effort and the care people put into making a reasonable and informed decision.
